title: Goodwill Letter for Late Payment: Free Template + When It Works
meta_description: Free goodwill letter for late payment template, plus when creditors say yes, where to send it, how to follow up, and when to dispute instead.
quick_answer: A goodwill letter for late payment is a polite request asking the creditor that reported an accurate late payment to remove it from your credit reports as a courtesy. Creditors don't have to agree. Odds are best for a one-time slip on an account that's now current, with an otherwise clean history. Send it to the creditor, not the bureaus. If the late payment is wrong, dispute it instead.
key_takeaways: A goodwill letter asks a creditor to remove an accurate late payment as a courtesy. Creditors don't have to agree, and some never do.
Your odds are best with a single slip, an otherwise strong history, and an account that's fully current before you ask.
Send it to the creditor that reported the late payment, by secure message or to its correspondence address, not to the credit bureaus. Follow up after about 30 days.
If the late payment is wrong, skip the goodwill letter and file a free dispute with the credit bureaus and/or the creditor.
You don't need to pay a credit repair company. You can do every step in this guide yourself for free.
Set autopay for at least the minimum due on every account. Check it again whenever you change banks or get a new card.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for anyone in the US who has an accurate late payment on their credit report, usually a one-time slip on an account that's now current, and wants to ask the creditor to remove it without paying a credit repair service.
intro:
One late payment can stay on your credit report long after you've fixed the problem. Maybe autopay broke when you switched banks, or a due date slipped by during a hectic month. If the late payment is accurate, one honest option is worth trying: a goodwill letter.

This guide explains what a goodwill letter is and when it has a realistic chance of working. It walks you through sending one, with a copy-paste template, a short version for secure messages, a follow-up plan and what to do if the answer is no. It also covers when to dispute instead, why you rarely need a paid service, and how to keep it from happening again.

The guide covers US credit reports. The rules are different in other countries. This is general information, not personal financial or legal advice. For decisions about your own situation, check the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) or talk to a reputable nonprofit credit counselor.

steps.name: Pull your credit reports
steps.text: Get your free reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion at AnnualCreditReport.com, the official site. Check the site for how often free reports are currently available. Note which creditor reported the late payment, the month and year, and how late it's shown (30, 60, 90 days or more). It may appear on one, two or all three reports.

steps.name: Confirm the late payment is accurate
steps.text: Compare the entry with your bank statements, payment confirmations and old account statements. If it's wrong, don't send a goodwill letter. Dispute it with the credit bureaus and/or the creditor instead (see the comparison table).

steps.name: Bring the account current
steps.text: Pay any past-due amount before you ask for anything. Creditors rarely approve a goodwill adjustment on an account that's still behind, and getting current stops more late payments from being reported.

steps.name: Find the right contact
steps.text: Use secure messaging in your online account or app, or the correspondence or customer service address on your statement or the creditor's website. Don't use the payment-only address. If you're not sure, call customer service and ask where to send a goodwill adjustment request.

steps.name: Write a short, honest letter
steps.text: Use the template below. Admit the late payment, give a one-sentence reason, explain what you've changed, and ask for removal as a courtesy. Keep it to one page. Include only the last four digits of your account number, and never include your Social Security number.

steps.name: Send it and keep a record
steps.text: If you use secure messaging, screenshot the confirmation that it was sent. If you mail it, use tracking or delivery confirmation. Write down the date, how you sent it and any reference number.

steps.name: Follow up after about 30 days
steps.text: If you haven't heard back, call or send a short secure message that mentions the date of your original request. If they approve it, ask for confirmation in writing. If they say no, politely ask whether anyone else reviews goodwill requests.

steps.name: Verify the change and prevent repeats
steps.text: Check all three credit reports over the next month or two to confirm the update. Then set up autopay for at least the minimum due, plus due-date alerts, so it doesn't happen again.

sections.heading: What is a goodwill letter for late payment?
paragraphs: A goodwill letter is a short, polite request asking a creditor, such as a card issuer, auto lender or loan servicer, to remove an accurate late payment from your credit reports as a courtesy. You aren't saying the creditor made a mistake. You're admitting the payment was late and asking them to overlook it.

Creditors are not required to remove a late payment that was reported accurately. US credit reporting law is built around accuracy, so a correct late payment can legally stay on your report. Removal is up to the creditor, and some lenders have a policy of never making goodwill adjustments.

It's still worth considering because there's little downside. It takes a few minutes, it doesn't trigger a credit inquiry, and some creditors do agree, especially for long-time customers with otherwise clean records. Think of it as asking a favor, not claiming a right.
bullets: Goodwill letter: you accept that the late payment is accurate and ask for it to be removed as a courtesy.
Credit bureau dispute: you say the information is wrong and ask for it to be investigated.
Who decides a goodwill request: the creditor that reported the late payment (called the 'furnisher'), not Equifax, Experian or TransUnion.
Cost and credit impact: free apart from postage, and no credit inquiry.

sections.heading: When a goodwill letter has the best chance of working
paragraphs: A goodwill letter has the best chance when three things are true: the late payment was a one-off, your history with that creditor is otherwise good, and the account is now current. Together they show the creditor a reliable customer who made one mistake and has already fixed the cause.

A specific, brief reason helps. Good examples are concrete without oversharing: 'My autopay stopped when I switched banks,' 'I was in the hospital the week it was due,' or 'My payment went to the old card number after a replacement card was issued.' One sentence is enough. You don't need to share medical or other private details.

Your odds drop sharply if you have several late payments, the account is still past due, or it's been charged off or sent to collections. In those cases, focus on getting current and building a run of on-time payments first. A letter sent later, with that record behind you, is a stronger request.
bullets: Better odds: one late payment, a long record of on-time payments, an open and current account, and a cause you've since fixed.
Lower odds: repeated late payments, an account that's still past due, an account closed for non-payment, a charge-off or collection, or a creditor that says it never makes goodwill adjustments.
Skip it: if the late payment is wrong. File a dispute instead.
Not sure? One polite letter rarely hurts. Just keep your expectations realistic.

sections.heading: Copy-paste goodwill letter template (plus a short online version)
paragraphs: Below is a one-page goodwill letter template you can copy, plus a shorter version for secure messages. Replace everything in brackets and delete anything that doesn't apply. A short, sincere letter is easier for a customer service team to read, approve or pass along.
[Your full name] | [Your mailing address] | [Phone and email] | [Date]
[Creditor name] | Attn: Customer Service – Goodwill Adjustment Request | [Correspondence address from your statement or the creditor's website]
Re: Goodwill adjustment request – account ending in [last 4 digits]
Dear [Creditor name] Customer Service Team,

I'm writing to ask for a goodwill adjustment to remove the late payment reported for [month and year] on my account ending in [last 4 digits]. I've been a customer since [year], and apart from this one payment, I have paid on time.

The payment was late because [one honest sentence, e.g., my automatic payment stopped when I changed banks, and I didn't notice until my next statement]. I take full responsibility for missing the due date. I paid the amount due on [date], and the account has been current since then.
To make sure this doesn't happen again, I have [set up automatic payments for at least the minimum due / added due-date alerts / moved my due date to match my payday].

I value my relationship with [Creditor name]. I'd be grateful if you would consider removing this late payment from my Equifax, Experian and TransUnion reports as a courtesy. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, [Signature if mailed] [Your printed name]

Short version for secure messaging or online forms: 'Hello, I'd like to request a goodwill adjustment on my account ending in [last 4 digits]. My [month and year] payment was reported late because [one-sentence reason]. I paid it on [date], the account has been current since then, and I've now [set up autopay]. I've paid on time since [year] apart from this payment. Would you consider removing this late payment from my credit reports as a courtesy? Thank you.'

If the late payment followed a hardship such as a job loss, illness or family emergency, say so in one sentence and mention that it's been resolved. The creditor doesn't need detailed medical or personal information to consider your request.
bullets: Use the exact month and year of the late payment as it appears on your credit report.
Take responsibility. Don't argue that the entry is wrong. If it is wrong, file a dispute instead.
Include only the last four digits of your account number, and never include your Social Security number.
If you polish the letter with a writing or AI tool, take out account details and other personal information first.
Keep a copy of exactly what you sent and the date you sent it.

sections.heading: Where to send it, how to follow up, and what to do if they say no
paragraphs: Send your goodwill letter to the creditor that reported the late payment, not to the credit bureaus, because only the creditor can change what it reports. Use the correspondence or customer service address on your statement or the creditor's website. Don't use the payment address, which is often a processing center that only handles checks.

Secure messaging in your online account or app is often the fastest option, and it gives you a timestamped record. You can also call first and ask, 'Do you review goodwill adjustment requests, and where should I send one?' If you mail your letter, use tracking or delivery confirmation.

Follow up if you haven't heard back in about 30 days. Call or send a short secure message that mentions the date of your original request and asks for an update. Keep follow-ups polite and spaced out. Sending the same letter over and over rarely helps.

If the answer is no, politely ask whether another department reviews goodwill requests or whether they'll reconsider. If the answer is final, accept it for now. Some people try once more after a longer run of on-time payments, but the creditor doesn't have to revisit its decision.

If the creditor agrees, ask for written confirmation. Then check all three credit reports over the next month or two. Updates usually show up after the creditor's next report to the bureaus, though timing varies. If the change never appears, contact the creditor and send a copy of its confirmation.
bullets: Log the date you sent it and how (secure message, mail or phone).
Log any tracking or reference number and the name of anyone you spoke to.
Log your follow-up date, about 30 days after sending.
Log the outcome and keep a copy of any written approval.
Log the date you confirmed the change on each of the three reports.

sections.heading: Goodwill letter vs. disputing a late payment with the credit bureaus
paragraphs: A goodwill letter asks a creditor to remove an accurate late payment as a courtesy. A dispute asks a credit bureau or creditor to correct information that's inaccurate or can't be verified. Which one you need depends entirely on whether the late payment is correct.

You have grounds for a dispute if you paid on time but were reported late, the dates or how late you were is wrong, or the account isn't yours. Under the US Fair Credit Reporting Act, you can dispute errors for free with each bureau that shows them and directly with the creditor. Bureaus generally have to investigate within about 30 days, sometimes longer, and correct or delete anything that can't be verified.

Some situations are worth a close look. For example, US mortgage rules generally say that for 60 days after your loan servicing moves to a new company, a payment that reaches the old servicer by the due date can't be treated as late. If something like that happened to you, a dispute is the right tool, not a goodwill letter. The CFPB explains these rules on its website.

Don't dispute a late payment you know is accurate in the hope it disappears. The creditor will usually verify it and the entry will stay. Knowingly false disputes also aren't a good-faith use of the process. Before you file any dispute, gather proof such as bank statements showing the payment cleared, confirmation numbers or letters from the creditor.
bullets: Late payment accurate? Send a goodwill letter.
Late payment wrong? Dispute it with the bureaus and/or the creditor, with documents to back you up.
Partly wrong (for example, shown as 60 days late when it was 30)? Dispute the inaccurate part.
Not sure? Compare your bank records with the credit report before you choose.

sections.heading: Why you usually don't need a credit repair company for this
paragraphs: Paying a credit repair company to send a goodwill letter is usually unnecessary, because you can write the same letter yourself in minutes for free. A company has no special power to make a creditor remove an accurate late payment. It sends the same kind of request you would.
The same goes for disputes. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says that anything a credit repair company can legally do for you, you can do yourself for little or no cost.

Be cautious with any company that promises to remove accurate negative information or wants money up front. The US Credit Repair Organizations Act generally bars credit repair companies from charging you before they've done the work they promised. If you want personal help with debt or budgeting, a reputable nonprofit credit counseling agency may cost less. Check its accreditation and fees first.
bullets: Red flag: a guarantee to remove accurate late payments or to raise your score by a set number of points.
Red flag: fees charged before any work is done.
Red flag: advice to dispute accurate information or to create a 'new' credit identity.
Red flag: pressure to sign quickly, or no written contract explaining your rights.

sections.heading: How long late payments stay on your credit report
paragraphs: In the US, a late payment generally stays on your credit reports for up to seven years from the date of the delinquency. After that, it should drop off on its own, with no letter needed.

The impact usually fades well before then. Scoring models generally give more weight to recent behavior, so one late payment from years ago typically matters less than one from last month, especially if you've paid on time since. How much it hurts depends on your overall credit profile and the scoring model, so be wary of anyone who quotes exact point drops.

Creditors typically don't report a payment as late to the bureaus until it's at least 30 days past due, though you may owe a late fee sooner. If you've only just missed a due date, paying right away may keep it off your reports entirely. Check your account terms.

For official, current details on reporting periods and your rights, see the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov. Outside the US, the rules and timelines are different, so check with your local regulator or the credit reference agencies in your country.
bullets: Typical reporting threshold: 30 or more days past due.
Maximum reporting period in the US: generally up to seven years.
Impact: strongest when recent, and it fades with steady on-time payments.
Official source: the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov.

sections.heading: Set up autopay and alerts so it doesn't happen again
paragraphs: The simplest way to prevent another late payment is to turn on autopay for at least the minimum due on every account. Even if you prefer to pay the full balance by hand, a minimum-payment autopay is a safety net for the month you forget.

Most card issuers and lenders let you set this up in your online account or app, usually under a menu like 'Payments,' 'AutoPay' or 'Automatic payments.' Menu names vary, so check your creditor's help pages.

Autopay only works if the money is there. Pay from an account that usually has a cushion, and set low-balance alerts so a failed payment doesn't add an overdraft or returned-payment fee on top. Check every autopay again when you change banks, get a replacement card or refinance. Those are the most common times autopay quietly stops working.
bullets: Turn on autopay for at least the minimum payment.
Add due-date and payment-confirmation alerts by email or text.
Ask whether you can move your due date closer to payday. Some issuers allow this.
Keep a cushion in the funding account and set low-balance alerts.
Keep a simple list of each account, its due date and how it gets paid. Leave out full account numbers.

recommendations.best_for: Checking the tone and grammar of your goodwill letter so it reads as polite, concise and professional. A one-page letter may only need the free version, but check what each plan includes on Grammarly's site.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone hoping it will improve their odds on its own. The creditor decides based on your payment history, not your writing, and you can proofread a short letter carefully without any tool. Remove account numbers and personal details before running the text through any online tool.

recommendations.best_for: People who already use Notion and want one private page to track their goodwill requests (dates, how they sent it, reference numbers, follow-up dates) next to a list of every account's due date and payment method.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone who doesn't already use it. A notes app, spreadsheet or paper list works just as well for a handful of accounts. Don't store full account numbers, passwords or your Social Security number in it.

faq.question: Do goodwill letters actually work for late payments?
faq.answer: Sometimes. Creditors don't have to remove accurate late payments, and some have policies against it, but others do approve goodwill adjustments for customers with strong histories and a single slip. There are no reliable public success rates, so treat a goodwill letter as worth trying, not guaranteed.

faq.question: Will sending a goodwill letter hurt my credit score?
faq.answer: No. A goodwill letter is just a message to your creditor. It doesn't trigger a credit inquiry or change your report. The worst likely outcome is that the creditor says no and the late payment stays where it is.

faq.question: How long should I wait for a response to a goodwill letter?
faq.answer: Give the creditor about 30 days, then follow up politely by phone or secure message. If they agree, the change may take a reporting cycle or more to show up, so check all three credit reports again a month or two later.

faq.question: Can I send a goodwill letter if the account is closed?
faq.answer: Yes, but your odds are generally lower, especially if the account was closed for non-payment or charged off. If you closed it yourself in good standing, a letter to the original creditor is still worth a try.

faq.question: What should I do if the creditor says no to my goodwill letter?
faq.answer: Politely ask whether another department reviews goodwill requests, and accept the answer if it's final. Keep paying on time, because the impact of a late payment usually fades. Some people make one more request after a longer run of on-time payments. Don't send the same letter repeatedly, and don't switch to disputing an entry you know is accurate.

faq.question: Is a goodwill letter the same as pay-for-delete?
faq.answer: No. Pay-for-delete usually means offering to pay a collection account in exchange for having it removed. A goodwill letter is a courtesy request about an account you've already brought current, and you don't offer anything in return. Collectors don't have to agree to pay-for-delete either.

conclusion: A goodwill letter is a free, honest way to ask a creditor to remove one accurate late payment, but the creditor doesn't have to say yes. Your best chance is when it was a one-off slip, your record is otherwise solid, and the account is current. Send a short, specific letter to the creditor, not the bureaus. Keep a record and follow up politely after about 30 days. If the late payment is actually wrong, dispute it for free with the credit bureaus and/or the creditor instead, and skip paid services that charge for what you can do yourself. Whatever the answer, set up autopay and alerts so it doesn't happen again. Rules differ outside the US. For official details on your rights and reporting timelines, see the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov, or talk to a reputable nonprofit credit counselor about your own situation.
